selection.why: It is significantly better on median and mean case span and reduces waiting by 98.3%, while service time also falls by 2.1% and utilisation has no directional interpretation. Unlike the other plans, it has no significant worsening measure.
selection.gain_reading: both: the code verdict is both, because waiting h/case falls 98.3% while service h/case also falls 2.1%; this is less work being performed as well as much less queueing, not simply the same work moving faster.

passengers.note: It removed the 5.5062 h batching component before repair; its effect is shared and therefore not individually attributable, but the handler made a real edit.
It grew resources by 100 and was judged helped; its significant contribution is shared with CBW-001, so it is not a no-effect or structural-no-op passenger.

selection.runner_up: — no alternative is acceptable: round1 has significant worsening of median case span by 25.3% and waiting by 53.4%, despite service falling 34.9%.
selection.caveat: Do not over-read this as proof that the same work was completed faster: service fell 2.1%, so the process did less work, and the plan changes outcomes for cases. Individual effects are also confounded because both surviving candidates share the measured repair changes.

note: `best` is the best MEASUREMENT in the run, which is usually not the last round. ⚠️ `statistically_tied_with_best` is the SELECTOR'S CANDIDATE POOL, not a set of indistinguishable results: a row is admitted either because it is not significantly worse than `best` on the median, or because it is decisively better on ONE directional measure while possibly far worse on the others. Read each row's `admitted_because` before describing it, and never call the list a tie. `per_candidate` is the winning plan's own account: what each surviving candidate contributed on waiting, duration, throughput and resources.
